title: Chukat: the red heifer (Numbers 19)
hookLine: a ritual that purifies the impure and defiles the pure; tradition says even Solomon couldn't explain it

lines: A RARE RED COW, BURNED TO ASH.
cards: Why is the sky blue? Why do we have to? Why?
Why? A small child can keep that up until the grown-up in the room runs out and says, because. Grown-ups tend to hope that with enough study, everything eventually has a because.
Then comes this week's portion, Chukat, and the ritual it opens with is one that Jewish tradition itself says nobody has fully explained. A rare red cow, burned to ash. The ash makes people pure.
And the people who prepare it become impure. A law with no because.

teach.b: The ritual, in paraphrase, goes like this. Find a red heifer, a young cow, completely red, with no blemish, that has never worn a yoke.
She is slaughtered outside the camp and burned, with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet thread thrown into the fire. Her ashes are kept and mixed with fresh water.
Anyone who has touched a dead body is sprinkled with that water on the third day and the seventh, and becomes pure again.
Then the twist: the priest who prepares it, and the one who burns it, become impure themselves, until evening. The same ashes that cleanse one person make another unclean.
The chapter opens with the words chukat ha-Torah, the statute of the Torah.

teach.h: CHOK: A LAW WITH NO STATED REASON.
teach.b: A chok, in the rabbis' vocabulary, is a law given without a stated reason, alongside mishpatim, laws anyone could work out, like don't steal.

teach.h: EVEN SOLOMON: IT WAS FAR FROM ME.
teach.b: A midrash says King Solomon, well-known for his wisdom, understood every law but this one, and quoted his own words from Ecclesiastes: I said, I will be wise, but it was far from me.
Another midrash tells of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. A non-Jew asks him about the ritual, and he gives a clever answer. Afterward his students say: you pushed him off; what do you tell us?
He says, in paraphrase: the dead don't make impure, and the water doesn't make pure.

teach.h: IT IS A DECREE, AND WE KEEP IT.
teach.b: It is a decree, and we keep it. Jewish thinkers have held different views since. Maimonides held that every commandment has a purpose, even when we can't see it.
Others treat the chok as a lesson in trust. Both keep the law.

how: Besides the weekly reading of Chukat, the red heifer chapter is read again on Shabbat Parah, a special Sabbath before Passover, recalling the purification once needed before the festival.

practice: Bring to mind something you've never been able to explain: a loss, a person you love who does something you can't fathom, a question about God or about yourself. Don't try to solve it now.
Hold it the way you'd hold a stone in your hand, and say to yourself, I don't understand this, and it's still here.

wordCard.voice: Chok. A statute, a law given without a stated reason. The red heifer is the classic chok: ashes that make one person pure and another impure.

orig.note: Hebrew: statute, a decree; the portion Chukat takes its name from chukat ha-Torah, the statute of the Torah (Numbers 19:2).

carryVoice: Your line: not everything explains itself. I don't know yet is an honest answer. Day four hundred fifty-six, done.
